tool.name: Amazon Web Services
tool.tagline: The largest cloud platform: compute, storage, databases, networking and more
tool.description: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the most widely used cloud platform, offering hundreds of managed services for compute, storage, databases, networking, messaging and security, billed per use. Engineers use it to run everything from single Lambda functions to global, multi-account production systems. Learning its core building blocks, identity model and networking pays off in almost any back-end, data or platform role.

concepts.name: Regions, Availability Zones and edge
concepts.summary: AWS is split into isolated Regions, each made of several Availability Zones, plus edge locations for content delivery.
concepts.why: Where a resource lives decides its latency, its failure blast radius, its price and which laws apply to its data.
concepts.body:
AWS runs in **Regions**: independent geographic areas such as `us-east-1` (N. Virginia) or `eu-central-1` (Frankfurt). Each Region contains three or more **Availability Zones** (AZs), each one or more data centers with separate power, cooling and networking, linked to the other AZs by fast, low-latency fiber. An AZ can fail without taking the Region down, which is why highly available designs spread across at least two AZs.

Every service has a scope, and knowing it saves a lot of confusion:

- **Global**: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, Organizations.
- **Regional**: S3 buckets, Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS, VPCs. Data stays in the Region unless you copy it out.
- **Zonal**: EC2 instances, EBS volumes, subnets. An EBS volume can only attach to instances in its own AZ.

**Edge locations** (hundreds of points of presence) serve CloudFront and Route 53 close to users. Local Zones and Outposts push compute further toward users or into your own data center.

AZ names such as `us-east-1a` are shuffled per account, so `1a` in your account may be a different building from `1a` in a partner's. When coordinating across accounts (for example for PrivateLink or capacity planning) use the **AZ ID**, such as `use1-az1`, which is the same everywhere.

Pick a Region by latency to users, data-residency rules, service and instance-type availability, and price, which differs between Regions.
concepts.code:
# All Regions enabled for this account
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output text
# eu-central-1  us-east-1  us-west-2 ...

# AZ names vs the stable AZ IDs in one Region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region eu-central-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId]' --output text
# eu-central-1a  euc1-az2
# eu-central-1b  euc1-az3
# eu-central-1c  euc1-az1
takeaways: Region = isolated geography; AZ = isolated data center group inside it
Services are global, regional or zonal; check the scope before designing
Spread across two or more AZs for availability, Regions for disaster recovery
Use AZ IDs, not names, when matching zones across accounts
pitfalls: Assuming us-east-1a is the same physical zone in every account.

quiz.q: Which resource is scoped to a single Availability Zone?
quiz.explain: EBS volumes live in one AZ and can only attach to instances there; S3 and DynamoDB are regional and IAM is global.

quiz.q: Why do multi-AZ architectures survive a data-center outage?
options: AZs are physically separate with independent power, cooling and networking
AZs share power but have separate networks
AWS automatically moves instances between AZs
Each AZ is in a different Region
quiz.explain: AZs are engineered as independent failure domains within a Region; AWS does not move your instances for you.

concepts.name: Accounts, root user and shared responsibility
concepts.summary: An AWS account is the billing and security boundary; lock away its all-powerful root user and know what AWS secures versus what you secure.
concepts.why: Most serious AWS breaches start with a leaked root or admin credential or a misread of who is responsible for what.
concepts.body:
An **AWS account** is a container for resources and the boundary for billing, quotas and security: by default nothing in one account can touch another. Mature setups use many accounts (per environment or team), which you will meet later with Organizations.

When you create an account you get the **root user**: the sign-up email and password. Root has unrestricted access, and IAM policies cannot limit it. Treat it as a break-glass credential:

- Enable MFA on it (AWS now enforces this), preferably a passkey or hardware key.
- Never create root access keys; delete any that exist.
- Use it only for the few tasks that require it, such as closing the account or changing some billing and support settings.
- Do daily work through IAM Identity Center or IAM roles instead.

The **shared responsibility model** splits security duties. AWS secures the cloud itself: facilities, hardware, the hypervisor and managed-service software. You secure what you put in it: identities and permissions, network rules, encryption choices, your data, and the operating system and patches on EC2 instances. The line moves with the service. On EC2 you patch the OS; on RDS AWS patches the database engine but you still choose who can connect; on Lambda AWS manages the runtime and you own the code and its permissions.

Misconfiguration (a public bucket, an over-broad policy, an open security group) is always on your side of the line.
concepts.code:
# Who am I, and in which account?
aws sts get-caller-identity
# { "UserId": "AROA...:alice", "Account": "111122223333",
#   "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Admin/alice" }

# Account-level security checks
aws iam get-account-summary \
  --query 'SummaryMap.[AccountMFAEnabled,AccountAccessKeysPresent]'
# [1, 0]   -> root has MFA, root has no access keys (what you want)

# Generate the credential report: every user, key age and MFA status
aws iam generate-credential-report
aws iam get-credential-report --query Content --output text | base64 -d | head -3
takeaways: The account is the security and billing boundary
Root: MFA on, no access keys, used only for root-only tasks
AWS secures the infrastructure; you secure configuration, identities and data
pitfalls: Running everyday tooling with root or a long-lived admin access key.

quiz.q: On an EC2 instance, who is responsible for applying operating-system security patches?
options: AWS, because it owns the hardware
AWS Support, if you have a plan
quiz.explain: With EC2 you manage the guest OS; AWS manages the physical host and hypervisor.

quiz.q: What is the recommended use of the root user?
options: Only the few tasks that require root, protected by MFA
Running the AWS CLI on laptops
quiz.explain: Root cannot be restricted by IAM, so it is reserved for root-only tasks and kept behind MFA.

concepts.name: The AWS CLI: profiles, SSO and --query
concepts.summary: Install AWS CLI v2, sign in with IAM Identity Center profiles, and shape output with --query and --output.
concepts.why: The CLI is the fastest way to inspect and script AWS, and the same credential setup is reused by every SDK.
concepts.body:
**AWS CLI v2** maps every API operation to a command: `aws <service> <operation> --param value`. Run `aws s3api put-object help` for any command's reference.

Credentials and settings live in `~/.aws/config` and `~/.aws/credentials`, organised into **profiles**. The recommended way to sign in is IAM Identity Center: `aws configure sso` writes a profile, `aws sso login` opens a browser, and the CLI caches short-lived credentials. `aws configure` with an access key also works but stores a long-lived secret on disk, which you should avoid. Pick a profile with `--profile dev` or `export AWS_PROFILE=dev`, and a Region with `--region` or `AWS_REGION`.

Output formats are `json` (default), `yaml`, `text` and `table`. Two flags look similar but differ:

- `--filters` is sent to the service and filters on the server (supported by many EC2 `describe-*` calls).
- `--query` is a **JMESPath** expression applied by the CLI to the response, for picking and reshaping fields.

The CLI follows pagination tokens automatically and returns everything; use `--max-items` to limit it. Set `AWS_PAGER=""` or `--no-cli-pager` in scripts so output isn't piped to `less`.

Higher-level helpers exist for some services, notably `aws s3 cp`, `aws s3 sync` and `aws s3 ls`, alongside the 1:1 API commands in `aws s3api`. Many mutating EC2 commands accept `--dry-run` to check permissions without doing anything.
concepts.code:
# ~/.aws/config written by `aws configure sso`
# [profile dev]
# sso_session = acme
# sso_account_id = 111122223333
# sso_role_name = DeveloperAccess
# region = eu-west-1
# [sso-session acme]
# sso_start_url = https://acme.awsapps.com/start
# sso_region = eu-west-1

aws sso login --profile dev
export AWS_PROFILE=dev AWS_PAGER=""

# Server-side filter, then client-side reshaping
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType]' --output table

aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[?starts_with(Name, `logs-`)].Name' --output text
# logs-prod  logs-staging
takeaways: Use profiles and IAM Identity Center (aws sso login) instead of stored access keys
--filters runs on the server; --query (JMESPath) runs in the CLI
aws s3 has convenience commands; aws s3api is the raw API
pitfalls: Hard-coding a long-lived access key in ~/.aws/credentials on a laptop or CI runner.

quiz.q: You need only the IDs of running instances. Which combination is most efficient?
options: --filters to select running instances on the server, --query to extract the IDs
quiz.explain: Server-side --filters reduces what is returned; --query then reshapes the response locally.

quiz.q: Which command signs a profile in through IAM Identity Center?
quiz.explain: aws sso login performs the browser-based Identity Center sign-in and caches temporary credentials.

concepts.name: IAM: users, groups, roles and principals
concepts.summary: IAM decides who can call which AWS API: principals authenticate, and policies attached to them authorize each request.
concepts.why: Every action in AWS, from the console to Lambda, is an API call checked by IAM, so it underpins everything else.
concepts.body:
**IAM** (Identity and Access Management) is global and free. Every API request is made by a **principal** and is denied unless a policy allows it.

The identity types:

- **IAM users**: a long-term identity with a console password and/or access keys. Today they are for exceptions, such as a third-party tool that cannot assume roles.
- **IAM groups**: collections of users to attach policies to. A group is not a principal; you can't sign in as one or name it in a resource policy.
- **IAM roles**: identities with no long-term credentials. A trusted principal or service *assumes* the role and gets temporary credentials. EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks, CI pipelines and humans from another account all use roles.
- **Federated users**: people signing in through IAM Identity Center or an external identity provider, ending up in a role.

The modern pattern: humans use IAM Identity Center (one login, permission sets mapped to roles in each account); workloads use roles; IAM users with access keys are rare and audited.

Resources are named by **ARNs**, `arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource`, for example `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orders-fn` (IAM has no Region) or `arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:111122223333:orders`.

The guiding rule is **least privilege**: grant only the actions and resources a principal needs, start narrow and widen with evidence. AWS managed policies like `ReadOnlyAccess` are convenient starting points but are usually broader than necessary.
concepts.code:
# A group for auditors, using an AWS managed policy
aws iam create-group --group-name auditors
aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name auditors \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/SecurityAudit

aws iam create-user --user-name legacy-scanner
aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name auditors --user-name legacy-scanner

aws iam list-attached-group-policies --group-name auditors \
  --query 'AttachedPolicies[].PolicyName' --output text
# SecurityAudit

aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[?starts_with(RoleName, `orders`)].Arn'
takeaways: Everything is denied unless a policy allows it
Roles give temporary credentials and are the default for workloads and people
Groups organise users but are not principals
ARNs identify resources in policies
pitfalls: Creating an IAM user with access keys for an application running on AWS, instead of a role.

quiz.q: A Lambda function needs to write to DynamoDB. What should provide its credentials?
options: An IAM user's access keys in environment variables
An IAM role assumed by the Lambda service (execution role)
quiz.explain: Workloads on AWS use roles; the service assumes the role and receives rotating temporary credentials.

quiz.q: Which of these can be named as a principal in a resource-based policy?
quiz.explain: Users, roles, accounts and services are principals; groups are only containers for users.

concepts.name: Writing IAM policies
concepts.summary: Read and write JSON policies: Effect, Action, Resource and Condition, identity versus resource policies, and how deny wins.
concepts.why: Least privilege is only as good as the policies you write, and most access bugs are policy bugs.
concepts.body:
A policy is a JSON document with a `Version` (always `"2012-10-17"`) and a list of statements. Each statement has:

- `Effect`: `Allow` or `Deny`.
- `Action`: API actions like `s3:GetObject`; wildcards such as `s3:Get*` work.
- `Resource`: the ARNs the actions apply to.
- `Condition` (optional): extra tests on request context keys, such as `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:PrincipalTag/team` or service keys like `s3:prefix`.

**Identity-based policies** attach to users, groups and roles; they have no `Principal`. **Resource-based policies** (S3 bucket policies, SQS queue policies, KMS key policies, role trust policies) attach to the resource and must name a `Principal`.

Policies come as AWS managed, customer managed (reusable, versioned) or inline (embedded in one identity). Prefer customer managed for anything you write yourself.

Evaluation basics: everything starts denied; an applicable `Allow` permits the action; an explicit `Deny` anywhere overrides every allow. That makes `Deny` statements good guardrails.

A classic gotcha is resource granularity. In S3, `s3:ListBucket` applies to the bucket ARN `arn:aws:s3:::bucket`, while `s3:GetObject` applies to objects, `arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*`. Put the wrong ARN in and you get AccessDenied despite the right action.

Write policies narrow, then use **IAM Access Analyzer** to validate them and to generate a least-privilege policy from the actions a role actually used in CloudTrail.
takeaways: Statement = Effect + Action + Resource (+ Condition)
Resource policies name a Principal; identity policies don't
Default deny, allow grants, explicit deny always wins
Bucket-level and object-level S3 actions need different ARNs
pitfalls: Granting s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::bucket (no /*), which matches no objects.

quiz.q: A role has an Allow for s3:* on a bucket and another attached policy with a Deny for s3:DeleteObject on it. Can it delete objects?
options: No, an explicit deny overrides any allow
It depends on which policy was attached first
quiz.explain: Explicit deny always takes precedence over allows, regardless of order.

quiz.q: Which policy type must contain a Principal element?
options: An inline policy on a role
A policy attached to a group
quiz.explain: Resource-based policies such as bucket policies say who they apply to via Principal.

concepts.name: EC2 instances, AMIs and instance types
concepts.summary: Launch virtual servers from AMIs, choose an instance type, configure them with user data and connect without opening SSH.
concepts.why: EC2 is the foundation many other services run on, and knowing its knobs explains most AWS compute pricing and behaviour.
concepts.body:
An **EC2 instance** is a virtual machine launched from an **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image: a root volume snapshot plus launch settings) into a subnet of a VPC, in one Availability Zone.

**Instance types** read like `m7g.large`: family `m` (general purpose; `c` compute, `r` memory, `t` burstable, `g`/`p` GPU), generation `7`, attribute `g` (AWS Graviton ARM; `i` Intel, `a` AMD), size `large`. Graviton types usually give the best price-performance if your software runs on ARM64. `t` types run on CPU credits and suit spiky, mostly idle workloads.

Launch settings you will always touch:

- **Security groups** (the firewall) and the **subnet** (which decides public or private).
- An **instance profile** (IAM role) so code gets credentials without keys.
- **User data**: a script that runs as root on first boot, typically to install and start your app.
- **IMDSv2 required** (`HttpTokens=required`) to protect the metadata service.

Connect with **SSM Session Manager** (needs the SSM agent, preinstalled on Amazon Linux, and the `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` policy) instead of SSH: no open port 22, no key pairs, and sessions are logged.

Lifecycle: *stop* keeps the EBS root volume (you stop paying for compute, not storage); *terminate* deletes the instance and, by default, its root volume. Data on **instance store** disks is lost on stop. Public IPv4 addresses are billed hourly, so avoid them where you can. Treat instances as replaceable: bake or script everything rather than hand-configuring servers.
concepts.code:
# Latest Amazon Linux 2023 AMI for ARM, from a public SSM parameter
AMI=$(aws ssm get-parameter \
  --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64 \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text)

ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI" --instance-type t4g.small \
  --subnet-id subnet-0a1b2c3d --security-group-ids sg-0a1b2c3d \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=ssm-core \
  --metadata-options HttpTokens=required \
  --user-data file://init.sh \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=web-1}]' \
  --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)

aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$ID"
aws ssm start-session --target "$ID"        # shell, no SSH port needed

aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids "$ID"       # keeps EBS data
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$ID"  # gone for good
takeaways: Instance = AMI + type + subnet + security groups + IAM role + user data
Read type names: family, generation, processor attribute, size
Use Session Manager instead of SSH keys and open ports
Stop keeps EBS volumes; terminate and instance store lose data
pitfalls: Storing important data on instance store volumes or hand-configuring a pet server you can't rebuild.

quiz.q: What does the g in m7g.large indicate?
quiz.explain: The attribute letter after the generation number denotes the processor; g means Graviton.

quiz.q: You stop (not terminate) an EBS-backed instance. What do you keep paying for?
quiz.explain: Compute billing stops, but attached EBS volumes still exist and are billed.

concepts.name: VPCs, subnets and route tables
concepts.summary: A VPC is your private network in a Region: carve its CIDR into per-AZ subnets and use route tables to make them public or private.
concepts.why: Nearly every resource that isn't fully serverless runs in a VPC, and networking mistakes are the most common cause of 'it can't connect'.
concepts.body:
A **VPC** is an isolated virtual network in one Region with an IPv4 CIDR block between `/16` and `/28` (for example `10.20.0.0/16`), optionally plus IPv6. Plan CIDRs that don't overlap with other VPCs or your offices, because overlapping ranges can't be peered or routed together later.

A **subnet** is a slice of the VPC's range in **one** Availability Zone. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet (network, router, DNS, a future-use address and broadcast), so a `/24` gives 251 usable IPs. Create subnets in at least two AZs.

Every subnet is associated with a **route table**. Routes are matched by longest prefix, and every table has a `local` route for the VPC CIDR, so all subnets can reach each other by default.

What makes a subnet public is only its routes:

- **Public subnet**: a route `0.0.0.0/0` to an **Internet Gateway** (IGW). Instances there also need a public IP to be reachable.
- **Private subnet**: no route to the IGW. Instances can't be reached from the internet; for outbound access they use a NAT gateway.

The standard layout is three tiers across two or three AZs: public subnets for load balancers and NAT gateways, private subnets for applications, and isolated subnets for databases.

Every account has a **default VPC** per Region with public subnets, handy for experiments but not for production. Use VPC **Flow Logs** to see accepted and rejected traffic when debugging.
concepts.code:
VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)

PUB=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC" --cidr-block 10.20.0.0/24 \
  --availability-zone eu-west-1a --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
PRIV=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC" --cidr-block 10.20.10.0/24 \
  --availability-zone eu-west-1a --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)

IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id "$VPC" --internet-gateway-id "$IGW"

# A route table with a default route to the IGW makes a subnet public
RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id "$VPC" --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW"
aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id "$RT" --subnet-id "$PUB"

aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids "$PUB" --query 'Subnets[0].AvailableIpAddressCount'
# 251
takeaways: A subnet lives in exactly one AZ; AWS reserves 5 IPs in each
Public vs private is decided by the route table (route to an IGW or not)
Choose non-overlapping CIDRs up front
Spread tiers across at least two AZs
pitfalls: Picking a tiny or overlapping VPC CIDR, which can't be fixed without rebuilding.

quiz.q: What makes a subnet 'public'?
options: A route table entry sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway
Its CIDR being in a public range
quiz.explain: Public is purely about routing to an IGW (plus instances having public IPs).

quiz.q: How many usable IPv4 addresses does a /28 subnet have in AWS?
quiz.explain: A /28 has 16 addresses and AWS reserves 5, leaving 11.

concepts.name: Security groups and network ACLs
concepts.summary: Security groups are stateful, allow-only firewalls on network interfaces; NACLs are stateless rules on subnets.
concepts.why: Correct firewall rules are the difference between a private database and a breach, and the first thing to check when traffic fails.
concepts.body:
A **security group** (SG) is a virtual firewall attached to network interfaces (instances, load balancers, RDS, Lambda in a VPC, ECS tasks). Its properties:

- **Allow rules only**. Anything not allowed is denied.
- **Stateful**: if inbound traffic is allowed, the response is automatically allowed out, and vice versa.
- New SGs allow all outbound and no inbound traffic.
- A rule's source can be a CIDR, a prefix list or **another security group**. Referencing SGs is the idiomatic way to build tiers: the database SG allows port 5432 *from the app SG*, so any instance in the app tier can connect regardless of its IP, and nothing else can.

Changes apply immediately to existing connections' future packets, and one interface can have several SGs (the rules are combined).

**Network ACLs** sit at the subnet boundary. They are **stateless**, have numbered rules evaluated in order, and support explicit **Deny**. Because they're stateless you must allow return traffic yourself, typically the ephemeral port range `1024-65535`. The default NACL allows everything, and most teams leave it that way, using SGs for real control and NACLs only for coarse subnet-wide blocks.

When something can't connect, check in this order: route tables, SG inbound on the target, SG outbound on the source, NACLs both ways, then the OS firewall and whether the process listens on the right interface. VPC Reachability Analyzer automates much of this.

Never open `0.0.0.0/0` to SSH, RDP or database ports.
concepts.code:
WEB=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name web-alb --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d \
  --description "Public HTTPS" --query GroupId --output text)
APP=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name app --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d \
  --description "App tier" --query GroupId --output text)

# Internet -> load balancer on 443
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id "$WEB" \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# Load balancer SG -> app on 8080 (no IPs involved)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id "$APP" \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group "$WEB"

aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules --filters Name=group-id,Values="$APP" \
  --query 'SecurityGroupRules[?!IsEgress].[FromPort,ReferencedGroupInfo.GroupId]' --output text
# 8080  sg-0web...
takeaways: Security groups: allow-only, stateful, attached to interfaces
Reference security groups as sources to build tiers
NACLs: stateless, ordered, can deny, apply to whole subnets
Debug connectivity: routes, SGs, NACLs, then the host
pitfalls: Adding a NACL rule for inbound traffic but forgetting the outbound ephemeral ports for responses.

quiz.q: An instance's SG allows inbound TCP 443 and has no outbound rules at all. Can clients get HTTPS responses?
options: No, outbound must allow the response
Only if the NACL allows it too and the SG has an outbound rule
quiz.explain: SGs track connections, so responses to allowed inbound traffic are always permitted.

quiz.q: What is the best way to let only the app tier reach the database on 5432?
options: Use a NACL deny for everything else
Allow 5432 from the app tier's security group
quiz.explain: Referencing the app SG grants exactly the members of that tier, independent of IPs.

concepts.name: S3: buckets, objects and storage classes
concepts.summary: Store any amount of data as objects in buckets, pick storage classes by access pattern, and automate tiering with lifecycle rules.
concepts.why: S3 is the backbone of AWS storage: static assets, backups, data lakes, logs and artifacts all end up there.
concepts.body:
**Amazon S3** stores **objects** (any bytes, up to 5 TB each, plus metadata) under **keys** in **buckets**. Bucket names are globally unique across all AWS accounts, but each bucket lives in one Region and data stays there unless you replicate it. S3 is designed for 99.999999999% durability by storing data redundantly across AZs.

There are no real folders: `reports/2026/q3.csv` is one key, and the console just groups by `/` prefixes. S3 has **strong read-after-write consistency**: after a successful write, any read or list sees it.

**Storage classes** trade storage price against access cost and latency:

- **Standard** for frequently accessed data.
- **Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects between tiers automatically based on access, for unknown or changing patterns.
- **Standard-IA** and **One Zone-IA** are cheaper to store but charge per GB retrieved and have a 30-day minimum.
- **Glacier Instant Retrieval**, **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** and **Glacier Deep Archive** are for archives, with retrieval from milliseconds to hours.

**Lifecycle rules** transition objects to colder classes and expire them after a time, by prefix or tag. **Versioning** keeps every version of an object, protecting against overwrites and deletes (a delete adds a delete marker); pair it with lifecycle rules that expire old versions or costs grow silently.

Upload large files with **multipart upload**, which the CLI and SDKs do automatically above a threshold. Use `aws s3 sync` for directories and `aws s3api` for full control.
concepts.code:
B=acme-reports-111122223333
aws s3 mb "s3://$B" --region eu-west-1
aws s3 cp report.csv "s3://$B/reports/2026/10/report.csv"
aws s3 sync ./site "s3://$B/site" --delete        # mirror a directory
aws s3 ls "s3://$B/reports/" --recursive --human-readable
# 2026-10-17 09:12:44   1.2 MiB reports/2026/10/report.csv

aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket "$B" \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket "$B" \
  --lifecycle-configuration '{"Rules": [{
    "ID": "tier-logs", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": "logs/"},
    "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"},
                    {"Days": 180, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}],
    "Expiration": {"Days": 730},
    "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {"NoncurrentDays": 30}}]}'
takeaways: Buckets are regional with globally unique names; objects are key + bytes + metadata
Prefixes are just key strings, not folders
Choose storage classes by access pattern; automate with lifecycle rules
Versioning protects data but needs noncurrent-version expiration
pitfalls: Moving small, frequently read objects to Standard-IA, where retrieval fees and minimums cost more than they save.

quiz.q: After a successful PUT of a new object, a GET for it immediately follows. What does S3 return?
options: Possibly a 404 for a few seconds
The new object, because S3 is strongly consistent
quiz.explain: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all objects.

quiz.q: Data is written once, rarely read, and must be kept 7 years at the lowest cost. Which class fits?
quiz.explain: Deep Archive is the cheapest storage for long-term, rarely accessed data, with retrieval in hours.

concepts.name: Block and file storage: EBS and EFS
concepts.summary: Attach EBS volumes to instances for disks, snapshot them for backups, and use EFS when many machines need a shared file system.
concepts.why: Databases, build caches and legacy apps need real disks and file systems, and choosing the wrong one costs money or availability.
concepts.body:
**EBS** volumes are network-attached block devices for EC2. A volume lives in **one AZ** and normally attaches to one instance at a time; it persists independently of the instance.

Volume types:

- **gp3**: the default general-purpose SSD. It includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, and you can buy more IOPS and throughput independently. Prefer it over the older gp2, where performance scaled with size.
- **io2 Block Express**: provisioned-IOPS SSD for demanding databases, with higher durability.
- **st1 / sc1**: throughput-optimised and cold HDD for big sequential workloads.

You can grow a volume or change its type online with `modify-volume`, then extend the partition and file system inside the OS.

**Snapshots** are point-in-time, incremental backups stored regionally in S3. Restore one to create a volume in any AZ of the Region, or copy it to another Region for disaster recovery. Volumes restored from snapshots load blocks lazily, so first reads are slow unless you pre-warm or use Fast Snapshot Restore. Turn on **EBS encryption by default** for the account; AWS Backup or Data Lifecycle Manager can schedule snapshots.

**EFS** is a managed NFS file system that many instances, containers and Lambda functions mount at once, across AZs. It grows and shrinks automatically and bills per GB stored, with Elastic throughput by default. Use it for shared content, not as a database disk. Windows shares, Lustre and NetApp ONTAP are available as **FSx**.

**Instance store** disks are physically attached and very fast, but vanish when the instance stops.
concepts.code:
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default

VOL=$(aws ec2 create-volume --availability-zone eu-west-1a --size 100 \
  --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250 --query VolumeId --output text)
aws ec2 wait volume-available --volume-ids "$VOL"
aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id "$VOL" --instance-id i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 --device /dev/sdf

# Grow online, then on the instance: sudo xfs_growfs /data
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id "$VOL" --size 200

SNAP=$(aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id "$VOL" --description nightly \
  --query SnapshotId --output text)
aws ec2 copy-snapshot --region eu-central-1 \
  --source-region eu-west-1 --source-snapshot-id "$SNAP"   # DR copy

# Shared file system for many instances or containers
aws efs create-file-system --encrypted --throughput-mode elastic \
  --tags Key=Name,Value=shared-media --query FileSystemId --output text
# fs-0a1b2c3d   ->  sudo mount -t efs fs-0a1b2c3d:/ /mnt/shared
takeaways: EBS = one-AZ block device; gp3 is the default with tunable IOPS and throughput
Snapshots are incremental, regional, and copyable across Regions
EFS = shared NFS across AZs for many clients
Instance store is fast but ephemeral
pitfalls: Expecting an EBS volume to attach to an instance in another AZ; restore a snapshot there instead.

quiz.q: Ten containers in three AZs must read and write the same files. What should you use?
quiz.explain: EFS is a multi-AZ shared file system; EBS volumes are single-AZ and normally single-attach.

quiz.q: You need a volume's data in a different AZ. How?
options: Detach and attach it to an instance there
Snapshot it and create a new volume from the snapshot in the target AZ
Change the volume's AZ with modify-volume
Copy it with aws s3 cp
quiz.explain: Volumes are tied to their AZ; snapshots are regional and can create volumes in any AZ.

concepts.name: RDS: managed relational databases
concepts.summary: Run PostgreSQL, MySQL and other engines with managed backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and read replicas.
concepts.why: Most applications need a relational database, and RDS removes the undifferentiated work of running one.
concepts.body:
**Amazon RDS** runs relational engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2) for you. You choose the engine, instance class and storage; AWS handles provisioning, OS and engine patching in maintenance windows, automated backups and monitoring. You don't get OS access.

Networking: create a **DB subnet group** of private subnets in at least two AZs, keep the database **not publicly accessible**, and allow the port only from the application's security group. Connect using the **endpoint hostname**, never an IP, because the IP changes during failover.

Availability and scaling are separate features:

- **Multi-AZ** keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ. If the primary or its AZ fails, RDS fails over automatically (typically in a minute or two) and the endpoint points to the new primary. In the classic instance deployment the standby serves no reads; a Multi-AZ DB cluster adds two readable standbys.
- **Read replicas** are asynchronous copies, possibly in other Regions, that serve read traffic. They can lag, and you can promote one to a standalone database.

**Backups**: automated backups with point-in-time restore (retention up to 35 days) plus manual snapshots kept until you delete them. Restores always create a *new* instance.

Other essentials: `--manage-master-user-password` keeps the admin password in Secrets Manager; parameter groups hold engine settings; storage autoscaling grows disks; **RDS Proxy** pools connections, which matters for Lambda and other bursty clients; and **deletion protection** prevents accidents.
concepts.code:
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name app-db \
  --db-subnet-group-description "Private DB subnets" \
  --subnet-ids subnet-db-a subnet-db-b

aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --engine postgres --db-instance-class db.m7g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 --storage-type gp3 --storage-encrypted \
  --multi-az --no-publicly-accessible \
  --master-username app --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids sg-db \
  --backup-retention-period 7 --deletion-protection

aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier orders-db
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier orders-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].Endpoint.Address' --output text
# orders-db.c1abc2def3gh.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com

aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica --db-instance-identifier orders-db-ro \
  --source-db-instance-identifier orders-db
takeaways: RDS manages patching, backups and failover; you manage schema, queries and access
Multi-AZ is for availability; read replicas are for read scaling
Private subnets, SG-to-SG access, connect by endpoint name
Point-in-time restore creates a new instance
pitfalls: Expecting the classic Multi-AZ standby to serve read traffic; use read replicas for that.

quiz.q: The primary's AZ fails. What lets the application recover automatically?
options: A read replica in the same AZ
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ fails over to a synchronous standby and repoints the endpoint.

quiz.q: Reporting queries are slowing the primary. What helps without changing availability setup?
options: Add a read replica and send reports to it
quiz.explain: Read replicas offload read traffic; Multi-AZ standbys (classic) don't serve reads.

concepts.name: Lambda functions
concepts.summary: Run code without servers: write a handler, give it an execution role, and let events invoke it, paying only per request and duration.
concepts.why: Lambda is the glue and often the backbone of AWS architectures, from APIs to file processing and automation.
concepts.body:
A **Lambda function** is code plus configuration that AWS runs on demand. You write a **handler**, for Python `def handler(event, context)`, where `event` is a dict describing what happened (an HTTP request, an S3 upload, a batch of SQS messages) and `context` carries metadata such as the remaining time.

Configuration that matters:

- **Runtime** (`python3.13`, `nodejs22.x`, `java21` and others) or a **container image** up to 10 GB.
- **Memory** from 128 MB to 10,240 MB; CPU scales with it, so more memory often makes functions faster and no more expensive.
- **Timeout** up to 15 minutes. Long jobs belong elsewhere (Step Functions, ECS).
- **Execution role** for AWS permissions, and environment variables for configuration.
- **Architecture**: `arm64` (Graviton) is usually cheaper per GB-second.

Invocation models: **synchronous** (API Gateway, function URLs, direct invoke; the caller waits), **asynchronous** (S3, SNS, EventBridge; Lambda queues the event and retries failures twice), and **event source mappings** where Lambda polls SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams and invokes with batches.

Each concurrent request runs in its own **execution environment**. Code outside the handler runs once per environment (on a **cold start**) and is reused by later warm invocations, so create SDK clients and load config there, but never keep request-specific state in globals.

Logs from `print` or `logging` go to CloudWatch Logs automatically. Deploy with the CLI, SAM, CDK or Terraform:

```bash
zip fn.zip app.py
aws lambda create-function --function-name hello --runtime python3.13 \
  --architectures arm64 --handler app.handler --zip-file fileb://fn.zip \
  --role arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orders-fn
```
concepts.code:
# app.py
import json

INVOCATIONS = 0   # module scope: survives between warm invocations

def handler(event, context):
    global INVOCATIONS
    INVOCATIONS += 1
    name = (event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}).get("name", "world")
    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "headers": {"content-type": "application/json"},
        "body": json.dumps({"hello": name, "invocation": INVOCATIONS}),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":   # quick local test
    print(handler({"queryStringParameters": {"name": "Ada"}}, None)["body"])
    # {"hello": "Ada", "invocation": 1}

# aws lambda invoke --function-name hello --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out \
#   --payload '{"queryStringParameters": {"name": "Ada"}}' out.json
takeaways: Handler(event, context); the event's shape depends on the trigger
Memory also sets CPU; timeout max is 15 minutes
Init code outside the handler runs once per execution environment
Sync, async and polled (event source mapping) invocation behave differently
pitfalls: Keeping per-request data in global variables, which leaks into later invocations on a warm environment.

quiz.q: Where should a boto3 client used by every invocation be created?
options: At module level outside the handler
quiz.explain: Module-level code runs once per execution environment and is reused by warm invocations.

quiz.q: A CPU-heavy function at 128 MB takes 8 seconds. What is a sensible first experiment?
options: Increase memory, which also increases CPU
quiz.explain: CPU is allocated proportionally to memory, so more memory can cut duration and even cost.

concepts.name: How AWS pricing works
concepts.summary: Understand the billing dimensions (compute time, storage, requests, data transfer), set budgets, and find what is costing money.
concepts.why: Cloud bills are driven by architecture choices; engineers who understand pricing avoid nasty surprises.
concepts.body:
AWS charges per use, along a few recurring **dimensions**:

- **Compute time**: per second or hour for instances, containers and databases; per request and GB-second for Lambda.
- **Storage**: per GB-month (S3, EBS, snapshots, backups), sometimes plus provisioned IOPS.
- **Requests**: API calls to S3, DynamoDB, SQS, API Gateway, KMS.
- **Data transfer**: inbound from the internet is free; outbound to the internet is charged per GB; traffic **between AZs** is charged in both directions; traffic between Regions is charged.

Some charges surprise people because nothing seems to be "running": NAT gateways (hourly plus per GB), public IPv4 addresses (hourly), unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots, CloudWatch Logs ingestion and indefinite retention, idle load balancers, and forgotten dev databases.

Tools:

- **AWS Pricing Calculator** to estimate before building.
- **AWS Budgets** to alert on actual or forecast spend; create one on day one.
- **Cost Explorer** to break spend down by service, account, Region, usage type or tag.
- **Cost allocation tags** (such as `team`, `env`, `project`) must be activated in the billing console before they appear in reports, and only apply from then on.
- **Free Tier**: new accounts get free-tier credits and allowances, and some services have always-free monthly amounts (for example, a million Lambda requests).

Prices differ by Region and change over time; check the pricing page for each service rather than memorising numbers.
concepts.code:
# Alert by email when forecast monthly spend exceeds 80% of $200
aws budgets create-budget --account-id 111122223333 \
  --budget '{"BudgetName": "monthly-total", "BudgetType": "COST", "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
             "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "200", "Unit": "USD"}}' \
  --notifications-with-subscribers '[{
     "Notification": {"NotificationType": "FORECASTED", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
                      "Threshold": 80, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
     "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "ops@example.com"}]}]'

# Top services last month
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' \
  --output text | sort -t$'\t' -k2 -nr | head -5

# Classic waste: volumes attached to nothing
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query 'Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size,VolumeType]' --output text
takeaways: Bills are compute time + storage + requests + data transfer
Cross-AZ, cross-Region and internet egress traffic cost money
Set a budget alert immediately; use Cost Explorer and activated tags to attribute spend
Watch idle resources: NAT gateways, IPv4 addresses, volumes, logs
pitfalls: Leaving CloudWatch log groups on 'never expire' retention.

quiz.q: Which traffic is normally free?
options: Data from an EC2 instance to the internet
Data into AWS from the internet
quiz.explain: Inbound data transfer is free; outbound, cross-AZ and cross-Region transfer are charged.

quiz.q: You tag resources with team=search but the tag doesn't appear in Cost Explorer. Why?
options: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the billing console first
Tags take a year to appear
Cost Explorer can't group by tag
quiz.explain: User-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags, and apply from activation onward.

concepts.name: CloudWatch metrics, logs and alarms
concepts.summary: Collect metrics and logs, query logs with Logs Insights, and alarm on what matters.
concepts.why: You can't operate what you can't see; CloudWatch is the default place AWS services report their health.
concepts.body:
**CloudWatch metrics** are time series identified by a **namespace** (`AWS/EC2`, `AWS/ApplicationELB`, or your own), a name and **dimensions** (such as `InstanceId`). AWS services publish metrics automatically: EC2 every 5 minutes (1 minute with detailed monitoring), most others every minute. EC2 doesn't report memory or disk usage from inside the OS; install the **CloudWatch agent** for that. Publish your own business metrics with `PutMetricData` or, more cheaply, the Embedded Metric Format in logs.

**Alarms** watch a metric statistic over periods and move between `OK`, `ALARM` and `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`. Use "M out of N" datapoints to avoid flapping, choose how missing data is treated, and trigger actions: an SNS topic for paging, Auto Scaling policies, or EC2 recovery. Composite alarms combine others to reduce noise. Alarm on symptoms users feel (5xx rate, latency, queue age) rather than every cause.

**CloudWatch Logs** organises logs into **log groups** (per application) and **streams** (per source). Lambda, ECS with `awslogs`, API Gateway and many services write here directly. Set a **retention policy** on every group; the default is to keep logs forever and you pay for that.

**Logs Insights** queries log groups with a pipe-based language (`fields`, `filter`, `stats`, `sort`, `parse`), ideal during incidents. **Metric filters** turn log patterns into metrics you can alarm on, and **subscription filters** stream logs to Lambda, Firehose or OpenSearch. **Dashboards** put the key graphs for a service in one place.
concepts.code:
# Page when the ALB's targets return more than 10 5xx per minute, 3 of 5 minutes
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name orders-api-5xx \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB --metric-name HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/web-alb/0123456789abcdef \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 5 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \
  --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data notBreaching \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:eu-west-1:111122223333:oncall

aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /ecs/orders-api --retention-in-days 30

# Errors per 5 minutes over the last hour
QID=$(aws logs start-query --log-group-name /ecs/orders-api \
  --start-time $(date -d '-1 hour' +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, @message
    | filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() as errors by bin(5m)' \
  --query queryId --output text)
sleep 5; aws logs get-query-results --query-id "$QID"

aws cloudwatch put-metric-data --namespace Shop --metric-name OrdersPlaced \
  --dimensions Env=prod --value 1 --unit Count
takeaways: Metrics = namespace + name + dimensions; EC2 memory needs the agent
Alarm on user-facing symptoms with M-of-N datapoints
Set log retention on every log group
Logs Insights for ad-hoc queries; metric filters to alarm on log patterns
pitfalls: Alarming on every CPU spike, training the team to ignore pages.

quiz.q: You need to alarm when EC2 memory usage exceeds 90%. What is required?
options: Install the CloudWatch agent to publish memory metrics
quiz.explain: The hypervisor can't see guest memory usage; the agent publishes it from inside the OS.

quiz.q: What does --datapoints-to-alarm 3 with --evaluation-periods 5 achieve?
options: The alarm fires after 15 consecutive minutes
The alarm fires if any 3 of the last 5 periods breach
quiz.explain: M-of-N evaluation tolerates the odd quiet period while still catching sustained problems.

concepts.name: Roles, trust policies and STS
concepts.summary: A role pairs a trust policy (who may assume it) with permission policies; STS hands out temporary credentials when it is assumed.
concepts.why: Roles are how instances, functions, containers, CI and other accounts get credentials without any secret to leak.
concepts.body:
A **role** has two policy sides:

- The **trust policy** (a resource-based policy on the role) says which principals may call `sts:AssumeRole`: a service like `lambda.amazonaws.com`, another account, a specific role, or a federated identity provider such as GitHub Actions OIDC.
- **Permission policies** say what the role can do once assumed.

**STS** (Security Token Service) returns temporary credentials: an access key ID, secret key and **session token**, valid by default for one hour (up to the role's maximum session duration, at most 12 hours; role chaining is capped at one hour). Nothing long-lived exists to steal.

How services use roles:

- **EC2**: an *instance profile* wraps the role; the SDK fetches rotating credentials from the instance metadata service. Require IMDSv2, which uses session tokens and blocks common SSRF tricks.
- **Lambda**: the *execution role*.
- **ECS**: the *task role* is what your code uses; the *task execution role* is what ECS itself uses to pull images and write logs. Mixing them up is a common bug.

**Cross-account access**: account B creates a role trusting account A; principals in A need permission to call `sts:AssumeRole` on it. For third-party SaaS that assumes into your account, require an `sts:ExternalId` condition to prevent the confused-deputy problem.

The CLI and SDKs assume roles automatically when a profile has `role_arn` and `source_profile`, refreshing credentials as they expire. CI systems should use OIDC federation (`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`) instead of stored keys.
concepts.code:
cat > trust.json <<'EOF'
{"Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow",
                "Principal": {"Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com"},
                "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"}]}
EOF
aws iam create-role --role-name orders-fn \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name orders-fn \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole

# Assume a role in another account by hand
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/Deployer \
  --role-session-name alice --query Credentials.Expiration --output text
# 2026-10-17T13:04:11+00:00

# ...or let a profile do it automatically
# [profile prod]
# role_arn = arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/Deployer
# source_profile = dev
takeaways: Trust policy = who can assume; permission policy = what it can do
STS credentials expire (default 1 hour) and carry a session token
ECS task role is for your code; task execution role is for ECS itself
Use ExternalId for third parties and OIDC federation for CI
pitfalls: Putting the permissions a container needs on the ECS task execution role instead of the task role.

quiz.q: Account A's CI role must deploy into account B. What is required?
options: A role in B trusting A, and permission in A to call sts:AssumeRole on it
Only a trust policy in B
Only a policy in A allowing sts:AssumeRole
Sharing B's root access keys with A
quiz.explain: Cross-account assumption needs both sides: B's trust policy and A's identity permission.

quiz.q: Where does an EC2 instance's application get its role credentials?
options: From the instance metadata service via the instance profile
quiz.explain: The SDK credential chain reads rotating credentials from IMDS for the attached instance profile.

concepts.name: boto3: the Python SDK
concepts.summary: Use boto3 clients, the credential chain, paginators, waiters and ClientError handling to automate AWS from Python.
concepts.why: Most automation, Lambda code and glue scripts on AWS are written against an SDK, and boto3 is the most common one.
concepts.body:
**boto3** is the AWS SDK for Python, built on `botocore`. Create a **client** with `boto3.client("s3")`: it exposes every API operation as a snake_case method taking keyword arguments and returning a plain dict. The older **resource** interface (`boto3.resource`) offers objects like `Bucket`, but AWS no longer adds features to it, so prefer clients in new code.

Credentials come from the **default credential chain**, the same one the CLI uses: explicit arguments, environment variables, the shared config and credentials files (including SSO and assume-role profiles), container credentials (ECS, EKS Pod Identity) and finally the EC2 instance metadata service. Your code should not mention keys at all; the environment decides.

Patterns to know:

- **Paginators**: list calls return one page (S3 returns up to 1,000 keys). `client.get_paginator("list_objects_v2")` iterates all pages for you.
- **Waiters**: `client.get_waiter("instance_running").wait(...)` polls until a state is reached.
- **Errors**: service errors raise `botocore.exceptions.ClientError`; branch on `e.response["Error"]["Code"]`, for example `NoSuchKey`, `ThrottlingException`, `ConditionalCheckFailedException`.
- **Retries**: configure with `botocore.config.Config(retries={"mode": "standard"})` or `"adaptive"`.

Clients are thread-safe and somewhat expensive to create: build them once, at module level in Lambda, and reuse. Sessions (`boto3.Session(profile_name="dev")`) are not thread-safe; use one per thread when you need different credentials.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="eu-west-1",
                  config=Config(retries={"mode": "standard", "max_attempts": 5}))
s3.create_bucket(Bucket="acme-demo-123",
                 CreateBucketConfiguration={"LocationConstraint": "eu-west-1"})
for i in range(3):
    s3.put_object(Bucket="acme-demo-123", Key=f"logs/{i}.txt", Body=b"hi")

pages = s3.get_paginator("list_objects_v2").paginate(Bucket="acme-demo-123", Prefix="logs/")
print([o["Key"] for page in pages for o in page.get("Contents", [])])
# ['logs/0.txt', 'logs/1.txt', 'logs/2.txt']

try:
    s3.head_object(Bucket="acme-demo-123", Key="missing.txt")
except ClientError as e:
    print(e.response["Error"]["Code"])   # 404
takeaways: Prefer clients; responses are plain dicts
Never put keys in code; rely on the credential chain
Use paginators for any list call and waiters for state changes
Catch ClientError and branch on the error code
pitfalls: Calling list_objects_v2 once and assuming you got every key.

quiz.q: A script lists a bucket with 5,000 objects using a single list_objects_v2 call. What happens?
options: It returns at most 1,000 keys plus a continuation token
quiz.explain: List calls are paginated; use a paginator to follow the continuation tokens.

quiz.q: Where should a Lambda function create its boto3 client?
options: Inside the handler on every invocation
At module level, so warm invocations reuse it
quiz.explain: Module-level clients are created once per execution environment and reused across invocations.

concepts.name: KMS and Secrets Manager
concepts.summary: Encrypt data with KMS keys and envelope encryption, and keep credentials in Secrets Manager instead of code or config.
concepts.why: Encryption at rest and secret handling are baseline requirements for any production or regulated workload.
concepts.body:
**AWS KMS** manages encryption keys inside hardware security modules; key material never leaves KMS unencrypted. Key types: **AWS owned** (invisible, used by some services), **AWS managed** (`aws/s3`, `aws/ebs`: free, automatic, but you can't edit their policies or share them across accounts) and **customer managed** keys (about $1 per month, full control over key policy, rotation and grants).

`Encrypt` handles at most 4 KB, so real data uses **envelope encryption**: `GenerateDataKey` returns a data key twice, as plaintext and encrypted under the KMS key. You encrypt locally with the plaintext key, throw it away, and store the encrypted key next to the data. To read, call `Decrypt` on the small encrypted key. S3, EBS, RDS and DynamoDB do exactly this when you choose SSE-KMS, which is why one checkbox gives you encryption with auditable key use in CloudTrail.

Access to a key needs the **key policy** to allow it (directly or by delegating to IAM). Enable automatic rotation on customer managed keys; old material is retained so existing ciphertext still decrypts.

**Secrets Manager** stores secrets such as database passwords and API tokens, encrypted with KMS, versioned with staging labels (`AWSCURRENT`, `AWSPENDING`), with built-in rotation for RDS and Aurora, and optional cross-Region replication. Applications fetch secrets at runtime with their role and cache them. **SSM Parameter Store** `SecureString` is a cheaper option for configuration values that don't need rotation.

Never put secrets in environment variables of templates, AMIs, container images or Git.
concepts.code:
import json, boto3

sm = boto3.client("secretsmanager", region_name="eu-west-1")
sm.create_secret(Name="prod/orders/db",
                 SecretString=json.dumps({"user": "app", "password": "s3cr3t"}))
db = json.loads(sm.get_secret_value(SecretId="prod/orders/db")["SecretString"])
print(db["user"])                      # app

kms = boto3.client("kms", region_name="eu-west-1")
key_id = kms.create_key(Description="orders data")["KeyMetadata"]["KeyId"]

# Envelope encryption: use the plaintext key locally, store only the blob
dk = kms.generate_data_key(KeyId=key_id, KeySpec="AES_256")
print(len(dk["Plaintext"]))            # 32 bytes, never persist this
blob = dk["CiphertextBlob"]            # store next to the encrypted data

plain = kms.decrypt(CiphertextBlob=blob)["Plaintext"]
print(plain == dk["Plaintext"])        # True
takeaways: KMS keys never leave KMS; data is encrypted with data keys (envelope encryption)
Customer managed keys give you key policy, rotation and cross-account control
Secrets Manager stores, versions and rotates secrets; fetch and cache at runtime
pitfalls: Using an AWS managed key (aws/ebs) for snapshots you later need to share with another account.

quiz.q: Why does S3 encrypt objects with data keys rather than calling KMS Encrypt on the whole object?
options: Data keys are free while KMS keys are not
KMS Encrypt only accepts up to 4 KB, and envelope encryption avoids sending data to KMS
It is required for S3 versioning
quiz.explain: Direct Encrypt is limited to 4 KB; envelope encryption keeps bulk data local and KMS calls small.

quiz.q: Which store offers built-in automatic rotation for an RDS master password?
quiz.explain: Secrets Manager has managed rotation for RDS and Aurora credentials.

concepts.name: NAT gateways, endpoints and egress
concepts.summary: Give private subnets outbound internet with NAT gateways, reach S3 and DynamoDB privately with gateway endpoints, and keep egress costs sane.
concepts.why: Private workloads still need to pull packages and call APIs, and NAT data charges are a classic surprise on the bill.
concepts.body:
Instances in private subnets have no route to the internet. For **outbound-only** access, put a **NAT gateway** in a public subnet and add `0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-...` to the private subnets' route table. Return traffic flows back; nothing on the internet can open a connection in.

Design points:

- A NAT gateway lives in one AZ. For resilience create one **per AZ**, and route each AZ's private subnets to their local NAT, so an AZ failure doesn't cut egress elsewhere and you avoid cross-AZ data charges.
- You pay per hour *and* per GB processed. Heavy traffic through NAT (container image pulls, S3 transfers, logs) gets expensive.
- For IPv6, use an **egress-only internet gateway** instead: IPv6 addresses are globally unique, so no translation is needed.
- NAT instances (an EC2 doing NAT) are cheaper but you own their availability.

Reduce NAT traffic with **VPC endpoints**:

- **Gateway endpoints** for S3 and DynamoDB: free, added as routes (via a managed prefix list) to the route tables you choose. Traffic to those services never touches the NAT.
- **Interface endpoints** (PrivateLink) for most other services such as ECR, SQS, STS, Secrets Manager and CloudWatch Logs: an ENI with a private IP in your subnets, billed per hour and per GB but often cheaper than NAT for heavy use, and required for fully isolated subnets.

Endpoint policies can restrict what can be done through the endpoint, for example only buckets in your organization.
concepts.code:
EIP=$(aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc --query AllocationId --output text)
NAT=$(aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-pub-a --allocation-id "$EIP" \
  --query NatGateway.NatGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 wait nat-gateway-available --nat-gateway-ids "$NAT"

# Private subnets in AZ a send internet-bound traffic to the local NAT
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-priv-a \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id "$NAT"

# Free gateway endpoint: S3 traffic bypasses the NAT entirely
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-priv-a rtb-priv-b

aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids rtb-priv-a \
  --query 'RouteTables[0].Routes[].[DestinationCidrBlock || DestinationPrefixListId, NatGatewayId || GatewayId]' \
  --output text
# 10.20.0.0/16  local
# 0.0.0.0/0     nat-0a1b...
# pl-6da54004   vpce-0c2d...
takeaways: NAT gateway = outbound-only internet for private subnets; one per AZ
NAT is billed per hour and per GB processed
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and skip the NAT
Interface endpoints give private access to most other AWS APIs
pitfalls: Pulling large container images or S3 data through a NAT gateway instead of using endpoints.

quiz.q: Private instances download terabytes from S3 each month through a NAT gateway. What cuts the cost most simply?
options: Move instances to a public subnet
Add an S3 gateway endpoint to the private route tables
quiz.explain: Gateway endpoints for S3 are free and route that traffic around the NAT.

quiz.q: Why deploy one NAT gateway per AZ?
options: NAT gateways can only serve one subnet
So an AZ outage doesn't break egress in other AZs, and to avoid cross-AZ charges
quiz.explain: A NAT gateway is zonal; per-AZ NATs keep failure domains and data paths local.

concepts.name: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB and NLB
concepts.summary: Spread traffic across healthy targets in several AZs with an Application Load Balancer (HTTP) or Network Load Balancer (TCP/UDP).
concepts.why: Load balancers are the front door of almost every highly available service on AWS.
concepts.body:
**Elastic Load Balancing** offers three types:

- **Application Load Balancer (ALB)**: layer 7. Routes HTTP and HTTPS by host, path, header or query string; supports WebSockets, gRPC, redirects, fixed responses, OIDC authentication and AWS WAF. Targets can be instances, IP addresses (containers) or Lambda functions.
- **Network Load Balancer (NLB)**: layer 4. TCP, UDP and TLS with very high throughput and low latency, one static IP per AZ (or your Elastic IPs), and client source IPs preserved. Use it for non-HTTP protocols, static IP needs, and PrivateLink services.
- **Gateway Load Balancer**: for inserting third-party firewalls and appliances.

The pieces: a load balancer in subnets of at least two AZs (public for internet-facing, private for internal), **listeners** (protocol and port, with rules), and **target groups** that hold targets and define **health checks**. Unhealthy targets stop receiving traffic. When a target is removed, the **deregistration delay** (300 s by default) lets in-flight requests finish.

Terminate TLS on the load balancer with a free certificate from **ACM**, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Put a security group on the ALB and let targets accept traffic only from that SG.

Cross-zone load balancing spreads requests evenly across all targets in all AZs; it is always on for ALBs and off by default for NLBs, where enabling it adds inter-AZ data charges.

Make health-check endpoints cheap and honest: they should fail when the instance truly can't serve, but not when a shared dependency is down, or every target fails at once.
concepts.code:
TG=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --name web-tg --protocol HTTP --port 8080 \
  --vpc-id vpc-0a1b2c3d --target-type ip --health-check-path /healthz \
  --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)

LB=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name web-alb --type application \
  --subnets subnet-pub-a subnet-pub-b --security-groups sg-0web \
  --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)

aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn "$LB" --protocol HTTPS --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:111122223333:certificate/abcd-1234 \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn="$TG"

aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn "$LB" --protocol HTTP --port 80 \
  --default-actions 'Type=redirect,RedirectConfig={Protocol=HTTPS,Port=443,StatusCode=HTTP_301}'

aws elbv2 register-targets --target-group-arn "$TG" --targets Id=10.20.10.15 Id=10.20.11.22
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TG" \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].[Target.Id,TargetHealth.State]' --output text
# 10.20.10.15  healthy
# 10.20.11.22  initial
takeaways: ALB for HTTP routing, NLB for TCP/UDP, static IPs and PrivateLink
Listener -> rules -> target group -> health-checked targets
Terminate TLS on the LB with ACM; targets accept traffic only from the LB's SG
Health checks should reflect the target, not shared dependencies
pitfalls: A health check that queries the database, so a DB blip marks every target unhealthy at once.

quiz.q: You need to route /api/* to one service and /static/* to another on the same domain. Which load balancer?
quiz.explain: Path-based routing is a layer-7 feature of the ALB.

quiz.q: A partner needs to allow-list fixed IP addresses for your TCP service. What fits?
options: NLB with Elastic IPs per AZ
quiz.explain: NLBs provide static IPs per AZ, optionally your own Elastic IPs.

concepts.name: EC2 Auto Scaling
concepts.summary: Run a self-healing, elastic fleet: launch templates, Auto Scaling groups across AZs, target tracking and instance refresh.
concepts.why: Auto Scaling turns individual servers into a fleet that replaces failures and follows demand without manual work.
concepts.body:
An **Auto Scaling group** (ASG) keeps a number of instances running between `min` and `max`, aiming at `desired`. It launches them from a **launch template** (AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM profile, user data; templates are versioned) into subnets you list, balancing across AZs.

ASGs heal: if an instance fails its health check it is terminated and replaced. Set the health check type to **ELB** when you attach target groups, so an instance whose app is broken (but whose VM is fine) is replaced too, and give it a **grace period** to boot.

Scaling policies change `desired`:

- **Target tracking**: keep a metric near a target, such as average CPU at 50% or `ALBRequestCountPerTarget` at 1,000. The default choice.
- **Step scaling**: add or remove capacity in steps based on CloudWatch alarm thresholds.
- **Scheduled actions**: known patterns, such as scaling up before business hours.
- **Predictive scaling**: forecasts from history and scales ahead of the curve.

Rolling out a new AMI is an **instance refresh**: the ASG replaces instances in batches while keeping a minimum healthy percentage. **Mixed instances policies** combine several instance types and On-Demand with Spot capacity for big savings. **Lifecycle hooks** pause instances while launching or terminating, for example to drain work or register with other systems; **warm pools** keep pre-initialised instances for fast scale-out.

The ASG only works if instances are disposable: no state on local disks, configuration fully automated, and logs shipped off the box.
concepts.code:
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name web --launch-template-data '{
  "ImageId": "ami-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890", "InstanceType": "m7g.large",
  "SecurityGroupIds": ["sg-0app"], "IamInstanceProfile": {"Name": "web-app"},
  "MetadataOptions": {"HttpTokens": "required"}}'

aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --launch-template 'LaunchTemplateName=web,Version=$Latest' \
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-priv-a,subnet-priv-b" \
  --target-group-arns "$TG" --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 120

aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --policy-name cpu-50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{"TargetValue": 50,
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {"PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"}}'

# Roll out a new launch template version
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --auto-scaling-group-name web \
  --preferences '{"MinHealthyPercentage": 90}'
takeaways: ASG = launch template + subnets in several AZs + min/desired/max
Use ELB health checks so broken apps get replaced
Target tracking is the default scaling policy
Instance refresh rolls out new AMIs safely
pitfalls: Using EC2 health checks only, so instances with a crashed app keep running and failing requests.

quiz.q: An ASG with min 2, max 10 uses target tracking at 50% CPU; average CPU rises to 90%. What happens?
options: Nothing until someone changes desired capacity
The ASG increases desired capacity to bring CPU back toward 50%
Instances are resized to a larger type
quiz.explain: Target tracking adjusts desired capacity automatically within min and max.

quiz.q: What is the role of the health check grace period?
options: It limits how often instances are refreshed
It gives new instances time to boot before health checks can mark them unhealthy
quiz.explain: Without it, instances still starting up could be killed for failing health checks.

concepts.name: Containers on ECS and Fargate
concepts.summary: Run Docker images on AWS with ECR, ECS task definitions and services, using Fargate so there are no servers to manage.
concepts.why: ECS on Fargate is the simplest production path from a container image to a scalable, load-balanced service on AWS.
concepts.body:
**Amazon ECR** is the private image registry. Authenticate Docker with `aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --password-stdin <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com`, then tag and push. Enable scan on push and use lifecycle policies to expire old images.

**Amazon ECS** concepts:

- A **task definition** is the versioned blueprint: containers, image, CPU and memory, ports, environment, secrets (from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store), log configuration and health check, plus two IAM roles: the **task role** your code uses and the **task execution role** ECS uses to pull images, fetch secrets and write logs.
- A **task** is a running instance of a task definition.
- A **service** keeps N tasks running, registers them with a load balancer target group, replaces failed tasks, scales with Application Auto Scaling and performs deployments.
- A **cluster** groups services and capacity.

Capacity comes from **Fargate** (serverless: pay per task vCPU and memory, no instances to patch) or **EC2** capacity providers (cheaper at scale, GPUs, more control). Fargate Spot runs interruptible tasks at a discount.

With the `awsvpc` network mode (required on Fargate) each task gets its own ENI, private IP and security group, so SG-to-SG rules work per service.

Deployments are rolling by default; enable the **deployment circuit breaker** with rollback so a bad image is automatically reverted. ECS Service Connect adds service discovery and traffic metrics between services.
concepts.code:
{
  "family": "orders-api",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "runtimePlatform": {"cpuArchitecture": "ARM64", "operatingSystemFamily": "LINUX"},
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/orders-api-task",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "api",
    "image": "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:1.4.2",
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080}],
    "secrets": [{"name": "DB_PASSWORD",
      "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/orders/db-AbCdEf:password::"}],
    "logConfiguration": {"logDriver": "awslogs", "options": {
      "awslogs-group": "/ecs/orders-api", "awslogs-region": "eu-west-1",
      "awslogs-stream-prefix": "api"}},
    "healthCheck": {"command": ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1"],
                    "interval": 30, "retries": 3}
  }]
}
takeaways: ECR stores images; ECS runs them from versioned task definitions
Service = desired count + load balancer + deployments
Task role for your code, task execution role for ECS itself
Fargate removes servers; awsvpc gives each task its own ENI and SG
pitfalls: Using mutable tags like latest in task definitions, so you can't tell or roll back what is running.

quiz.q: Your container can't read from S3 but logs and image pulls work. Which role most likely lacks permission?
quiz.explain: Application calls use the task role; the execution role is only for ECS's own actions such as pulling and logging.

quiz.q: What does the deployment circuit breaker do?
options: Stops a failing deployment and can roll back to the last working version
Limits CPU usage of new tasks
quiz.explain: It detects tasks that repeatedly fail to become healthy and rolls back.

concepts.name: Route 53: DNS, alias records and routing
concepts.summary: Host DNS zones, point names at AWS resources with alias records, and steer traffic with weighted, latency and failover routing.
concepts.why: DNS is how users find your service, and Route 53's routing policies are a key tool for releases and disaster recovery.
concepts.body:
**Route 53** is AWS's DNS service. A **hosted zone** holds records for a domain; public zones answer the internet, private zones answer only inside associated VPCs. To use a zone for a domain registered elsewhere, set the registrar's NS records to the four name servers Route 53 assigns.

Record types are the usual ones (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, CAA) plus a Route 53 extension, the **alias record**. An alias points a name at an AWS resource such as an ALB, CloudFront distribution, S3 website or another record. Unlike a CNAME it works at the zone apex (`example.com`), follows the target's changing IPs automatically, and queries to AWS targets are free.

**TTL** controls how long resolvers cache answers. Lower it a day before a planned migration; keep it moderate otherwise.

**Routing policies** let one name return different answers:

- **Weighted**: split traffic, for example 90/10 for a canary.
- **Latency**: answer with the Region closest in latency to the user.
- **Failover**: primary and secondary, switching when a health check fails.
- **Geolocation / geoproximity**: by user location, for compliance or localisation.
- **Multivalue**: up to eight healthy records, simple client-side balancing.

**Health checks** probe endpoints (or watch CloudWatch alarms) and remove unhealthy answers. Remember DNS failover is only as fast as TTLs and client caching allow; it is a Region-level tool, not a substitute for load balancers within a Region.
concepts.code:
cat > change.json <<'EOF'
{"Comment": "Point the API at the ALB",
 "Changes": [{"Action": "UPSERT",
   "ResourceRecordSet": {
     "Name": "api.example.com", "Type": "A",
     "AliasTarget": {
       "HostedZoneId": "Z32O12XQLNTSW2",
       "DNSName": "dualstack.web-alb-1234567890.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com",
       "EvaluateTargetHealth": true}}}]}
EOF
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ \
  --change-batch file://change.json --query ChangeInfo.Status --output text
# PENDING   (INSYNC within about a minute)

dig +short api.example.com
# 52.48.12.34
# 34.250.7.89
takeaways: Hosted zones hold records; delegate with NS records at the registrar
Alias records work at the apex and track AWS resources' IPs
Weighted, latency and failover policies steer traffic
DNS changes are bounded by TTL and client caching
pitfalls: Using a CNAME at the zone apex, which DNS forbids; use an alias record.

quiz.q: You want example.com (no www) to point at a CloudFront distribution. Which record?
options: An A record with the distribution's current IPs
An alias A record targeting the distribution
quiz.explain: Alias records work at the apex and follow the distribution's changing addresses.

quiz.q: Which routing policy sends 5% of traffic to a new stack?
quiz.explain: Weighted records split answers proportionally to their weights.

concepts.name: CloudFront CDN
concepts.summary: Serve content from edge locations with caching, HTTPS and private S3 origins via Origin Access Control.
concepts.why: A CDN cuts latency and origin load and is the standard way to serve static sites and assets from S3.
concepts.body:
**CloudFront** caches and serves content from hundreds of edge locations. A **distribution** has one or more **origins** (an S3 bucket, an ALB, API Gateway, any HTTP server) and **cache behaviors** that map path patterns (`/static/*`, `/api/*`, default `*`) to an origin with its own settings.

Caching is controlled by **cache policies** (TTLs and which headers, cookies and query strings form the cache key) and **origin request policies** (what to forward to the origin without affecting the key). Keep the cache key small; every extra header or cookie fragments the cache. For dynamic APIs use the managed `CachingDisabled` policy and still benefit from TLS termination and AWS's backbone network.

For a private S3 bucket, use **Origin Access Control (OAC)**: CloudFront signs requests to S3, and the bucket policy allows the `cloudfront.amazonaws.com` service principal only for your distribution's ARN. The bucket stays private with Block Public Access on. OAC replaces the older Origin Access Identity.

Other essentials:

- Custom domains need an ACM certificate created in **us-east-1**, and an alias record in Route 53.
- **Invalidations** remove cached objects but are slow-ish and billed beyond a free allowance; prefer versioned file names (`app.3f9c.js`) with long TTLs.
- **Signed URLs or cookies** restrict private content; AWS WAF attaches to block attacks.
- **CloudFront Functions** (lightweight JavaScript at the edge, for header rewrites and redirects) and **Lambda@Edge** (heavier logic) customise requests.
concepts.code:
# Bucket policy: only this CloudFront distribution may read objects (OAC)
cat > oac-policy.json <<'EOF'
{"Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [{
   "Sid": "AllowCloudFrontOAC",
   "Effect": "Allow",
   "Principal": {"Service": "cloudfront.amazonaws.com"},
   "Action": "s3:GetObject",
   "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-site/*",
   "Condition": {"StringEquals": {
     "AWS:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudfront::111122223333:distribution/E1ABCDEF2GHIJ"}}}]}
EOF
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket acme-site --policy file://oac-policy.json
